scenario: Your parallel-run has just started. The new tool receives mirrored writes but nobody sees its responses.
question: When can you start moving live traffic?

options.text: Once the mismatch rate has been zero for 48 continuous hours in shadow mode, then ramp in measured steps and hold each step until criteria stay green.
After one clean day, because the sandbox tests passed.
Immediately. Shadow mode already proved the tool works.

why: Shadow mode compares outputs field by field against the system of record. Advancing before it is clean skips the evidence the step exists to produce.

scenario: At a ramp step, one success criterion fails. The team wants to patch it and keep the percentage where it is.
question: What does the playbook say?

options.text: Pause the ramp, fix the cause and restart that step from zero.
Carry on to the next percentage. The failure was small.
Roll back the entire project and start the planning again.

why: A step only counts if criteria stay green for its full minimum run length. Restarting that step keeps the evidence honest without throwing away earlier progress.

scenario: It is T+30 minutes after cutover and the core workflow does not complete end-to-end. A rollback checkpoint is attached to that step.
question: What happens?

options.text: Follow the predefined rollback rule: if a checkpoint between T+0 and T+2h fails, revert DNS to the old system within 15 minutes.
Wait until T+4 hours to see if it fixes itself.
Ask every stakeholder to vote on what to do.

why: Rollback triggers and decision authority exist so the team acts in minutes instead of debating during an incident.

scenario: Cutover went well. Someone asks to switch off the old system today to save on licences.
question: What is the safe call?

options.text: Keep it read-only for stabilization, wait for user acceptance sign-off and keep it available for at least one billing cycle to recover stranded data.
Delete it now. A clean break avoids confusion.
Leave full write access open indefinitely.

why: Decommission is part of the migration. Stepping access down gradually, with sign-off first, stops the old system becoming a silent liability.

scenario: Two tools both claim to own customer records, and the mapping work is about to start.
question: What should be settled first?

options.text: A written system-of-record decision for each data entity, covering the owner, the rationale and the sync direction.
Let the new tool win by default since it is newer.
Sync both ways and fix conflicts when they appear.

why: The system of record decides which tool wins when data conflicts during reconciliation. Without a written decision every discrepancy becomes an argument.
